chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Sovereign Debt Actually Is

lessons.title: Why Countries Borrow: Deficits, Development, and the Sovereign Balance Sheet

children.text: Every February, when India's Finance Minister presents the Union Budget, one number gets almost as much airtime as any tax change: the fiscal deficit. For FY25, the government budgeted to borrow close to 4.9% of GDP just to cover the gap between what it collects and what it spends. That gap is not a one off. India's central government has run a fiscal deficit in effectively every year since Independence, and it is not alone. The United States, Japan, the United Kingdom, almost every large economy in the world carries a permanent stock of government debt. This lesson asks the question everything else in this course builds on: why do countries borrow at all, and why is a government's balance sheet nothing like a company's or a household's?
The Deficit Number Everyone Talks About

markDefs.definition: The gap between a government's total spending and its total revenue (tax plus non-tax) in a given year, before accounting for the borrowing used to bridge that gap.

children.text: A government's
fiscal deficit

is simply the gap between its total spending and its total revenue in a year, excluding the borrowing itself. When spending exceeds revenue, the government funds the difference from somewhere, and that somewhere is debt: government bonds, external loans, or, in an earlier era, printing money through the central bank, a route India has largely closed off since the FRBM Act of 2003. Run a fiscal deficit for one year and you have a manageable shortfall. Run one every year for decades, financed mostly by borrowing, and you get a growing stock of outstanding government debt, currently a little over 57% of GDP for the Centre alone, and closer to 80% of GDP once state government borrowings are added in.

children.text: Three Reasons Governments Borrow
Governments borrow for three broad reasons, and telling them apart matters, because they carry very different implications for whether the resulting debt is sustainable.

First, counter-cyclical spending. When the economy slows down, tax collections fall just as the government needs to spend more, on subsidies, income support, or stimulus, to cushion the slowdown. FY21 is the clearest recent example. Covid crushed GST and income tax collections at the exact moment the government needed to fund vaccine drives, the PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana foodgrain scheme, and support for MSMEs. The fiscal deficit spiked to 9.2% of GDP that year, roughly double the pre-pandemic norm.

Second, development spending. Building roads, ports, railways, and power infrastructure that the private sector will not fund at the scale or speed a growing country needs, especially early in its development. India's capital expenditure budget, which funds this kind of spending, has more than tripled since FY18, rising from around Rs 3 lakh crore to over Rs 11 lakh crore by FY25, with roads, railways, and defence taking the largest shares.

Third, and often overlooked: refinancing existing debt. Governments rarely repay old bonds out of current revenue. Instead, when a bond matures, they issue a new one to raise the cash needed to pay off the old one, a process called rollover. A large part of every year's borrowing programme is not new debt at all. It is old debt being refinanced at whatever interest rate the market happens to be charging that year, which is exactly why rising interest rates make existing debt more expensive to carry even if the government borrows no additional rupee.
How India Actually Finances Its Deficit

body.caption: How India's Fiscal Deficit Gets Financed (Approx. Shares)

cells: Bonds sold to banks, insurers, mutual funds, and increasingly foreign investors via the Fully Accessible Route (FAR)
Retail savings routed to the government through the National Small Savings Fund
World Bank, ADB, JICA and similar, usually tied to specific projects

body.text: Notice what's missing from that table: the RBI simply printing money to fund the deficit. India allowed this through automatic 'ad hoc Treasury Bills' before 1997, and the RBI still buys G-Secs in the secondary market through Open Market Operations, but it does not directly finance the government's deficit anymore. That separation, often called 'no monetisation of the deficit', is a deliberate guardrail against the kind of runaway inflation that direct central bank financing of governments tends to produce.

children.text: A Government's Balance Sheet Doesn't Work Like Yours
Here is where sovereign debt stops behaving like company or household debt, and understanding this distinction is the foundation for everything else in this course.

When a company borrows, a bank looks at its assets, inventory, receivables, plant and machinery, and its ability to sell those assets if things go wrong. A government's balance sheet does not work that way. Yes, India owns assets: forex reserves worth several hundred billion dollars, stakes in public sector companies like LIC and ONGC, land, and infrastructure. But a government cannot easily sell a highway, and it is not about to nationalise its way out of a debt crisis by auctioning off a state. Its real ability to repay debt rests on something far less tangible: its power to tax a growing economy over the next twenty, thirty, fifty years.

This is why sovereign debt is assessed completely differently from corporate debt. Analysts and rating agencies do not ask what a government could sell tomorrow. They ask whether the economy will grow fast enough, and whether the government will tax and spend responsibly enough, that debt stays a manageable share of a rising GDP. That is the entire logic behind the debt-to-GDP ratio you saw earlier, and it is the single most important number in sovereign risk analysis, one this course returns to constantly.

body.text: A government does not repay debt by selling assets. It repays debt by taxing a growing economy, year after year, for decades. Every sovereign risk question in this course eventually comes back to that one sentence.

children.text: Good Debt, Bad Debt
Not all government borrowing carries the same risk, and the distinction closely mirrors capital expenditure versus revenue expenditure in the Union Budget.

Debt used to fund capital expenditure, a new expressway, a metro line, a defence platform, builds an asset that, in theory, lifts future GDP, which is exactly what services the debt. Debt used to fund revenue expenditure, salaries, pensions, interest on old debt, subsidies with no productive kicker, buys nothing that grows the economy tomorrow. It simply moves consumption forward in time.

India's own budget arithmetic makes this tension visible every year. In FY25, interest payments alone consumed close to a quarter of the Centre's total expenditure, more than the entire capital expenditure budget. Every rupee going toward interest on old debt is a rupee not available for a new highway or hospital, and it is also a reminder that debt taken on for the wrong reasons in the past keeps taxing the present.

body.title: Good Debt or Bad Debt?
body.scenario: The Government of Karnataka issues a Rs 5,000 crore bond to fund two things: Rs 3,000 crore for a new suburban rail corridor in Bengaluru, and Rs 2,000 crore to clear a backlog of pending salary arrears owed to state government employees.
body.prompt: Using the capital versus revenue expenditure framework from this lesson, which portion of this borrowing is more likely to help service itself over time, and why?
body.modelAnswer: The Rs 3,000 crore rail corridor is capital expenditure: it builds an asset that should lift Bengaluru's economic activity, property values, and eventually tax revenue such as property tax and commercial GST, giving the state a growing base to help service that portion of the debt. The Rs 2,000 crore salary arrears is revenue expenditure: it clears a past obligation but creates no new income stream. That portion of the debt has to be serviced entirely out of whatever revenue growth the state achieves anyway. It does not help pay for itself the way the rail corridor might.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why is comparing a government's debt to its GDP more useful than comparing it to a fixed rupee ceiling?
options: Because GDP is easier for the government to measure than its own revenue
Because a growing economy can carry a larger absolute amount of debt while the debt burden, relative to the size of the economy, stays stable or falls
Because rating agencies only look at GDP and ignore government revenue entirely
Because it removes the effect of inflation completely
body.explanation: GDP is a rough proxy for a country's overall taxable capacity. As long as GDP grows faster than debt, the debt-to-GDP ratio can fall even while the absolute rupee amount of debt keeps rising, which is exactly what a healthy, growing economy should be able to do. This is also why the relationship between the interest rate on debt and the economy's growth rate, often written as 'r versus g', is so central to the sovereign debt sustainability lessons later in this course.

body.title: India's Centre Fiscal Deficit (% of GDP)

children.text: None of this borrowing happens in a vacuum. Every rupee the Indian government borrows gets priced by the market, in the yield investors demand on a 10-year G-Sec, and every fiscal deficit number gets scrutinised by rating agencies deciding whether India deserves an upgrade from its current BBB-minus rating. The next lesson looks at exactly who is on the other side of this transaction: who actually lends to a government, and why a G-Sec, a Eurobond, and a World Bank loan carry very different risk and cost even though they all fund the same deficit.

points: A fiscal deficit is the gap between government spending and revenue in a year. Financing that gap year after year builds up the stock of outstanding government debt.
Governments borrow for three broad reasons: counter-cyclical support during downturns, development or capital spending, and refinancing (rolling over) existing debt as it matures.
India finances its deficit mainly through market borrowing in G-Secs, supplemented by small savings schemes and limited external loans. The RBI does not directly monetise the deficit anymore.
A sovereign's ability to repay debt rests on its power to tax a growing economy over time, not on liquidating assets, which is why debt-to-GDP, not the absolute rupee amount, is the key metric.
Debt that funds capital expenditure tends to be more sustainable than debt that funds revenue expenditure, because it builds the asset base that eventually helps service it.

body.text: The fiscal deficit, debt-to-GDP, and expenditure figures in this lesson are approximate and drawn from recent Union Budget documents and RBI data. Figures change with every Budget and with revised estimates. Check the latest numbers at indiabudget.gov.in or the RBI's Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy before using them in analysis or advice.
